blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A planner wants renewal R12 in every plan and asks for a value of $10 billion on it instead of a new row. The other must-dos are equality rows, and the budget cannot cover R12 together with them. What does the solver report?

options.text: INFEASIBLE, since the large value makes R12 a must-do the budget cannot cover
options.says: A value is not a row: the page says a large weight hides the infeasible mandate behind an OPTIMAL plan.

options.text: OPTIMAL, with a plan that can leave R12 out when the must-dos take the money
options.says: Right: the weight only makes R12 attractive; when it cannot fit, the plan quietly drops it and still reports OPTIMAL.

options.text: OPTIMAL, with a plan that keeps R12 and drops other must-dos to make room
options.says: The other must-dos are equality rows, so no plan may drop them; R12, held only by its value, is what goes.

options.text: INFEASIBLE_OR_UNBOUNDED, since the solver cannot weigh the value against budgets
options.says: Nothing is unbounded here; the page says the plan comes back OPTIMAL without the project.

origin.section: Round 2: Business Rules Are Rows, Written Strong

questions.stem: A colleague writes 'B starts at least 3 years after A' as one row on the sums of t times the start variables, with a big-M term that switches it off when B is unfunded. Which plan does this row allow that the cumulative rows refuse?

options.text: A in 2027 and B in 2030, three years apart
options.says: Both forms allow it: three years is the lag.

options.text: A in 2027 and B in 2029, two years apart
options.says: Both forms refuse it: two years is less than the lag.

options.text: None, since the two forms agree on each plan
options.says: They disagree on one plan in the printed table: B funded while A is not.

options.text: B in 2028, with A not funded at all
options.says: Right: with A unfunded the row's right side is at most 0, so B may start in any year.

origin.section: Trap Questions: Rows That Look Right and Are Not

questions.stem: Two identical renewals may each start in 2027 or 2028, and the budget pays for one start a year. To break symmetry a colleague adds 'the first starts in year t whenever the second does', for each year. What happens to the best plan?

options.text: It drops to one renewal, since a plan with the two in different years keeps no copy
options.says: Right: the printed solve falls from 100 to 50; both copies of the two-year plan break the row.

options.text: It keeps both renewals, since the row just removes the copy with the order swapped
options.says: Both copies start the renewals in different years, and the row refuses both; the printed value falls to 50.

options.text: It keeps both renewals, since the solver breaks the symmetry before the row applies
options.says: The row is part of the model and refuses the plan; the printed best value with it is 50.

options.text: It becomes infeasible, since the row forces the two renewals into the same year
options.says: Funding only the first renewal satisfies the row; the printed solve returns a plan worth 50.
